$$\max_{\vec\alpha\,\geq\,0}\;\vec\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\,\vec\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\vec\alpha$$

Support vector machines: from a constrained problem to the points that decide it

Lagrange multipliers turn a constraint into a price. Applied to the widest possible margin between two classes, those prices vanish for almost every training point, and the handful that remain define the classifier.

Part A
Lagrangian optimisation
1

Constrained optimisation

Find the lowest point of a function — but only among the points that obey a rule.

The problem this whole topic is built around has two parts: a function to minimise and a condition the answer must satisfy.

$$\min_{w}\; f(w)\qquad \text{s.t.}\qquad g(w)\le 0$$
  • \(f(w)\) is the objective function — what we want to make small.
  • \(g(w)\) is the constraint function. The set of points it allows, \(\mathcal F=\{w : g(w)\le 0\}\), is the feasible set.

Without the constraint we would set \(\nabla f(w)=0\) and be done. With it, that stationary point may lie outside \(\mathcal F\), and the true answer may sit on the boundary \(g(w)=0\) where \(\nabla f\neq 0\). We can attack this directly, or find a reformulation that is easier to solve. The Lagrangian is that reformulation: it folds the constraint into the objective so that the outer problem over \(w\) has no constraint left.

The standard form and its conventions

Every problem in these notes is first rewritten into the shape above. Two conventions make that possible:

  • Always minimise. Maximising \(g(w)\) is the same as minimising \(-g(w)\), or — when \(g>0\) — minimising \(1/g(w)\). Block 12 uses the second trick.
  • Always write constraints as "something \(\le 0\)". A constraint \(g(w)\ge c\) becomes \(c-g(w)\le 0\). Block 13 does exactly this with the SVM constraint \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\).

Real problems have many constraints \(g_1(w)\le 0,\dots,g_n(w)\le 0\). The lecture develops the theory with one constraint for readability; everything generalises by giving each constraint its own multiplier, which is what the SVM needs — one constraint per training point.

Why the sign convention matters

The multiplier introduced in the next block is required to be non-negative. That requirement only makes sense if every constraint is written as \(g(w)\le 0\). Writing a constraint the other way round silently flips the sign of its multiplier and breaks every argument in blocks 3 to 7.

Convex and Concave Functions

Pick any two points in the domain and join them with a straight line. For a convex function, the function never rises above that line.

$$f\bigl(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\bigr)\;\le\;\lambda f(x_1)+(1-\lambda)f(x_2)\qquad\forall\,x_1,x_2\ \ \text{and}\ \ \forall\,\lambda\in[0,1]$$

Every symbol has a job. \(x_1\) and \(x_2\) are the two endpoints you chose. \(\lambda\) slides between them: \(\lambda=1\) sits on \(x_1\), \(\lambda=0\) sits on \(x_2\), and \(\lambda=\tfrac12\) is the midpoint. So \(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\) is a point between the endpoints, called a convex combination. The left side is the height of the function there; the right side is the height of the chord there. Convexity says the first is never the larger of the two.

A function is concave when the inequality runs the other way, \(\ge\): the function never dips below the chord. Equivalently, \(f\) is concave exactly when \(-f\) is convex, which is why maximising a concave function and minimising a convex one are the same kind of problem.

See it for yourself

Choose a function, then drag the two endpoints and the mixing weight. The teal dot is the left side of the definition and the rose dot is the right side; the gap between them is the inequality.

\(\lambda\,f(x_1)\)
\((1-\lambda)\,f(x_2)\)
\(\lambda f(x_1)+(1-\lambda)f(x_2)\) — the chord
\(f\bigl(\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\bigr)\) — the function
so at \(x_\lambda=\)0.00: function≤chord

Reading the picture

  • \(x^2\) never escapes above its chord, whatever you do to the sliders. That is convexity.
  • \(-x^2\) never drops below it. That is concavity. The dual function \(q(\alpha)\) of block 5 is always this shape.
  • \(|x|\) is convex even though it has a corner. Convexity needs no derivatives at all — which matters, since the hinge loss behind soft-margin SVMs has exactly such a kink.
  • \(x^3\) is neither. Keep both endpoints positive and it looks convex; keep both negative and it looks concave; straddle zero and the inequality flips. A single bad pair \((x_1,x_2,\lambda)\) is enough to disqualify a function, but no number of good pairs proves convexity — the definition asks for all of them.
  • \(\tfrac12x+1\) sits exactly on its chord, so both inequalities hold with equality. Affine functions are convex and concave at once, which is why affine constraints are so well behaved in block 13.

Strict convexity and easier tests

If the inequality is strict (\(<\) rather than \(\le\)) whenever \(x_1\neq x_2\) and \(0<\lambda<1\), the function is strictly convex: the chord touches only at its endpoints. This is what gives the SVM a single answer rather than a set of equally good ones, since \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) is strictly convex and so has a unique minimiser.

Why convexity is worth this much attention

For a convex function, every local minimum is a global minimum, so gradient descent cannot get stuck in a bad valley and a solver that stops at a flat point has genuinely finished. For a strictly convex one, that minimum is unique. And for a convex problem with Slater's condition, the duality gap is zero. None of Part C would work without it.

Convex sets

The same chord idea applies to sets rather than functions. A set \(\mathcal C\) is convex when the straight segment between any two of its members stays inside it:

$$x_1,x_2\in\mathcal C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2\in\mathcal C\qquad\forall\,\lambda\in[0,1]$$

Drag the two endpoints around each set and slide \(\lambda\) along the segment between them. Watch where the moving point goes.

distance from the origin: 0.00
2

The Lagrangian function

Add the constraint to the objective, scaled by a non-negative weight.

$$L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha\,g(w),\qquad \alpha\ge 0$$

The new variable \(\alpha\) is the Lagrange multiplier. We still optimise over \(w\), but \(L\) now also depends on \(\alpha\). A useful way to read \(\alpha\) is as a price per unit of violation: whenever \(g(w)>0\) the term \(\alpha\,g(w)\) charges for breaking the rule, and a larger \(\alpha\) charges more.

With \(n\) constraints there is one multiplier per constraint, collected into a vector \(\vec\alpha\):

$$L(w,\vec\alpha)=f(w)+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,g_i(w),\qquad \alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0$$

If we fix a \(w\), we can ask how large the Lagrangian can be made by choosing \(\alpha\):

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,L(w,\alpha)=\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)$$

The answer to that question, worked out in the next block, is what makes the whole construction work.

3

What maximising over α does

For a fixed \(w\), the inner maximum is either infinite or exactly \(f(w)\) — and which one depends only on whether \(w\) is feasible.

Case 1: \(g(w)>0\) — the constraint is violated

The term \(\alpha\,g(w)\) is a positive number times \(\alpha\). Since we are maximising, we increase \(\alpha\) without limit, which pushes \(L(w,\alpha)\to\infty\).

Case 2: \(g(w)\le 0\) — the constraint is satisfied

Now \(\alpha\,g(w)\le 0\) for every \(\alpha\ge 0\): any positive \(\alpha\) can only lower \(L\) (or leave it unchanged when \(g(w)=0\)). The best choice is \(\alpha=0\), which gives \(L(w,\alpha)=f(w)\).

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}L(w,\alpha)=\begin{cases}\;\infty, & g(w)>0\\[4pt] \;f(w), & g(w)\le 0\end{cases}$$

In effect, \(\max_{\alpha}\) builds an infinitely high wall around the feasible set and leaves \(f\) untouched inside it. The constraint has not disappeared — it has been turned into part of the objective.

4

The primal: a min–max problem

Minimise the result of block 3 over \(w\), and you get back exactly the problem you started with.

We originally wanted the \(w\) that minimises \(f(w)\) subject to \(g(w)\le 0\). Take the function from block 3 and minimise it over \(w\). The outer minimisation will never choose an infeasible \(w\), because those score \(\infty\); among feasible ones it sees exactly \(f(w)\). So the two problems have the same solution:

$$\underbrace{\min_{w}\, f(w)\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ g(w)\le 0}_{\text{original problem}} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \underbrace{\min_{w}\,\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)}_{\text{Lagrangian equivalent (primal)}}$$

The min–max form is called the primal. Its optimal value is written \(p^\star\) and its minimiser \(w^{\text{opt}}\) (also written \(w^\star\)). Notice the outer problem over \(w\) is now unconstrained — the only constraint left is the trivial \(\alpha\ge 0\) on the inner variable.

The constraint is there to punish infeasible points. Why not just fix one large penalty, say \(\alpha=1000\), and minimise \(f(w)+1000\,g(w)\) with no inner maximisation at all?

Because any fixed price can be outbid. A finite \(\alpha\) sets an exchange rate: one unit of violation costs \(\alpha\). If the objective improves faster than that rate, breaking the rule becomes profitable. Take \(f(w)=-2000\,w\) with the constraint \(w\le 1\), so \(g(w)=w-1\), and charge \(\alpha=1000\):

\(w\)\(f(w)\)penalty \(1000\,g(w)\)total
\(1\) (feasible, the true optimum)\(-2000\)\(0\)\(-2000\)
\(10\) (infeasible)\(-20000\)\(9000\)\(-11000\)
\(100\) (infeasible)\(-200000\)\(99000\)\(-101000\)

The minimiser happily pays the fine and runs off to infinity. Raising \(\alpha\) to \(10^6\) does not fix the idea — it only moves the threshold, and some problem will cross it. Set \(\alpha\) too low and infeasible points win; set it too high and feasible points are distorted, since the penalty keeps charging even where the constraint is comfortably satisfied.

The inner maximisation prices each \(w\) separately. Read \(\min_w\max_{\alpha\ge0}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)\) as a game between two players who move in order:

  • The minimiser picks \(w\) and wants the final score as small as possible.
  • The maximiser sees that \(w\), then picks \(\alpha\ge0\) and wants the score as large as possible.

The maximiser's best reply depends only on the sign of \(g(w)\).

The rule is obeyed, \(g(w)\le 0\). Every \(\alpha>0\) multiplies a non-positive number and drags the score down, which is the opposite of what the maximiser wants. Its best move is \(\alpha=0\), and the score is just \(f(w)\). The penalty switches itself off.

The rule is broken, \(g(w)>0\). Now \(\alpha\,g(w)\) grows without limit as \(\alpha\) grows, however small the violation — \(g(w)=0.01\) is enough. There is no ceiling on \(\alpha\), so the maximiser drives the score to \(\infty\).

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr)=\begin{cases}\;f(w), & g(w)\le 0\\[4pt] \;\infty, & g(w)>0\end{cases}$$

So the minimiser is choosing between a finite score on feasible points and \(\infty\) on infeasible ones, and must reject every infeasible \(w\). No number had to be guessed: the price is chosen after \(w\) is known, and it is whatever that particular \(w\) deserves. That is what makes it an exact penalty rather than an approximate one — and why there is no \(\alpha\) left to tune.

5

Swapping min and max: the dual

Doing the minimisation over \(w\) first often turns out to be much easier. The question is whether it gives the same answer.

We converted a minimisation into a min–max problem. Before going further, the we pose two questions.
  • The first is whether the order of min and max can be exchanged:
$$\min_{w}\,\Bigl(\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,L(w,\alpha)\Bigr)$$

Primal form

$$\min_{w}\;J(w)$$

the same thing, with \(J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)\) — the barrier of block 3

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\Bigl(\min_{w}\,L(w,\alpha)\Bigr)$$

Dual form

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\;q(\alpha)$$

the same thing, with \(q(\alpha)=\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)\) — the dual function

Naming the inner parts is what produces the compact forms. The inner maximisation of the primal is the barrier function

$$J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,L(w,\alpha)=\begin{cases}f(w), & g(w)\le 0\\[3pt] \infty, & g(w)>0\end{cases}$$

which charges nothing on the feasible side and an infinite penalty the moment the rule is broken. The inner minimisation of the dual is the dual function

$$q(\alpha)=\min_{w}\,L(w,\alpha)=\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr),$$

so the primal problem is \(\min_w J(w)\), with optimal value \(p^\star\) and minimiser \(w^{\text{opt}}\), and the dual problem is \(\max_{\alpha\ge 0}q(\alpha)\), with optimal value \(d^\star\) and maximiser \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\).

Four different optimisers appear in this section and they must be kept apart, since each belongs to a different step:

SymbolSolvesDepends on
\(w^{\text{opt}}\)the outer minimisation of the primalnothing — it is the primal answer
\(\hat\alpha(w)\)the inner maximisation of the primalthe \(w\) you fixed
\(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\)the outer maximisation of the dualnothing — it is the dual answer
\(\hat w(\alpha)\)the inner minimisation of the dualthe \(\alpha\) you fixed

In particular \(\hat\alpha(w)\) is not \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\). It is \(0\) wherever \(g(w)<0\), it is any \(\alpha\ge0\) at all wherever \(g(w)=0\) since the term contributes nothing there, and it does not exist where \(g(w)>0\) because the line climbs without bound. It is a by-product of the barrier, not a price selected by optimising anything.

Why the primal needs no multiplier

The statement is true because of how the primal function \(J(w)\) is mathematically constructed to automatically reject invalid solutions, without needing an external multiplier to force the issue at the very end. The primal problem is defined as minimising \(J(w)\), where

$$J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge0}\bigl[f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\bigr]$$

Why its minimiser is feasible. If you evaluate a \(w\) that violates the constraint, making \(g(w)>0\), the inner maximisation step \(\max_{\alpha\ge0}\) will push \(\alpha\) to infinity to make the expression as large as possible. This makes \(J(w)=\infty\). Because the outer goal is to minimise \(J(w)\), the equation inherently rejects any \(w\) that yields infinity. The ultimate minimiser \(w^{\text{opt}}\) is therefore forced to be a feasible solution, where \(g(w^{\text{opt}})\le0\).

Why it needs no multiplier at all. Since the minimiser is already feasible, look at what happens to the inner maximisation \(\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha)\). To maximise \(f(w^{\text{opt}})+\alpha\,g(w^{\text{opt}})\) when \(g\) is a negative number or zero, \(\alpha\) must be \(0\) to avoid dragging the total value down. The inner maximisation collapses, the entire multiplier term becomes zero, and exactly \(f(w^{\text{opt}})\) is left.

$$p^\star=J\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)=f\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

Because the optimal value \(p^\star\) ultimately drops down to just \(f(w^{\text{opt}})\), evaluating the primal at its optimal point requires no \(\alpha\) multiplier.

Why the dual retains the multiplier

The mechanics of the dual differ fundamentally from the primal because the order of operations is reversed, which changes how the maths treats constraints and penalties. In the dual problem

$$d^\star=\min_{w}L\bigl(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

the penalty multiplier \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) is locked in before evaluating the minimum over \(w\). Because \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) is just a fixed, finite number during this inner minimisation, there is no threat of an infinite penalty being applied to constraint violations.

The minimisation evaluates \(f(w)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\) and might find a specific point \(\hat w\) where the baseline function \(f(w)\) is so low that, even after adding the penalty cost \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\), the total sum is still smaller than at any strictly feasible point. Because the inner minimisation has this freedom to break the constraint and simply pay the charge, the chosen \(\hat w(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\) is not guaranteed to be feasible. If it is not, then \(g\bigl(\hat w(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\bigr)\) is a non-zero number, and the second term below does not vanish — it remains a crucial part of the equation:

$$d^\star=f\bigl(\hat w(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\bigr)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}\,g\bigl(\hat w(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\bigr)$$

This structural freedom — allowing the maths to accept a penalty in order to achieve a lower overall score — is the exact reason the dual's optimal value \(d^\star\) can fall below the primal's \(p^\star\).

The two loops, side by side

Both problems are evaluated from the inside out: the inner operation runs first, once for every candidate value of the outer variable, and the outer operation then picks the best of the numbers collected. Written as pseudocode, the only difference is which variable sits where.

Primal — \(\min_w\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)\)

for each candidate w:
    solve  max over α ≥ 0 of L(w, α)
    → this number is J(w)

pick the w with the smallest J(w)
    → call it w_opt

p* = J(w_opt)

Dual — \(\max_{\alpha\ge0}\min_w L(w,\alpha)\)

for each candidate α:
    solve  min over w of L(w, α)
    → this number is q(α)

pick the α with the largest q(α)
    → call it α_opt

d* = q(α_opt)

What the inner step actually costs

This is where the symmetry ends. The dual's inner step is a genuine optimisation — you must search over \(w\). The primal's inner step needs no search at all, because \(L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)\) is a straight line in \(\alpha\) and its slope settles the answer:

Primal, with the inner max worked out

for each candidate w:
    if g(w) ≤ 0:   J(w) = f(w)     best price is α = 0
    else:          J(w) = ∞        the line climbs forever

pick the w with the smallest J(w)

p* = J(w_opt)

And since no \(w\) scoring \(\infty\) can ever win, that collapses to

The same thing, with the infinities dropped

for each candidate w:
    if g(w) ≤ 0:   record f(w)
    else:          skip it

p* = smallest recorded value

Which is just "minimise \(f\) over the feasible set" — the problem we started with. That is the point of block 4: the min–max form is a faithful rewriting, not a new problem.

PrimalDual
Outer loop over\(w\)\(\alpha\)
Inner step\(\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)\to J(w)\)\(\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)\to q(\alpha)\)
Cost of the inner stepfree — check the sign of \(g(w)\)a full optimisation
Outer steptake the smallesttake the largest

Strong duality and the saddle point

When strong duality holds, the primal and dual align without any gap and both optimal values arrive at the same number. Under this condition the optimal parameters lock into a mathematical stalemate known as a saddle point:

$$L\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha\bigr)\;\le\;L\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)\;\le\;L\bigl(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)\qquad\forall\,w,\ \forall\,\alpha\ge0$$

This double inequality dictates exactly how the variables behave when isolated.

Right side — \(w\) is a minimiser
$$L\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)\le L\bigl(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

Hold the optimal penalty \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) constant, and moving \(w\) away from \(w^{\text{opt}}\) can only raise the total value.

Left side — \(\alpha\) is a maximiser
$$L\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha\bigr)\le L\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

Hold the optimal weights \(w^{\text{opt}}\) constant, and moving \(\alpha\) away from \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) can only lower it.

The point \(\bigl(w^{\text{opt}},\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)\) is a saddle because the surface rises in the \(w\) direction, like the front and back of a saddle, and falls away in the \(\alpha\) direction, like the sides where the legs hang. Since moving \(w\) only raises the value and moving \(\alpha\) only lowers it, neither variable can independently change to achieve a better result from its own perspective.

  • The second question is what the swap buys us and how to get \(w\) back from \(\alpha\).
Part C answers both for the SVM.

Weak duality: always true

The claim is that the best the dual can ever achieve is no better than the best the primal achieves: \(q(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\le f(w^{\text{opt}})\). Nothing in the argument below assumes convexity, differentiability, or anything else about \(f\) and \(g\).

Step 1 — the primal as an infinite penalty

Define a single function \(J\) that carries the constraint inside it, by charging an infinite penalty the moment the rule is broken:

$$J(w)=\begin{cases} f(w), & g(w)\le 0\\[3pt] \infty, & g(w)>0\end{cases}$$

Minimising \(J\) over all \(w\) is the same as minimising \(f\) over the feasible points only, because no infeasible \(w\) could ever win against a finite value. So

$$\min_{w}J(w)=p^\star=f\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr),$$

the optimal value of the original primal problem. This is the barrier of block 3 written as a formula rather than as an inner maximisation.

Step 2 — the Lagrangian as a relaxation

Now fix any constant \(\alpha\ge0\) and form

$$L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)$$

This is a relaxed version of the same problem: breaking the constraint now costs a finite amount, \(\alpha\) per unit of violation, instead of costing everything. The whole proof rests on comparing the relaxed problem with the strict one.

Step 3 — compare them pointwise

Take any \(w\) at all and ask which of \(L(w,\alpha)\) and \(J(w)\) is smaller. There are only two possibilities.

Constraint satisfied: \(g(w)\le 0\)

\(\alpha\ge0\) times a non-positive number is non-positive, so adding \(\alpha g(w)\) to \(f(w)\) can only lower it or leave it unchanged:

$$L(w,\alpha)\le f(w)=J(w)$$
Constraint violated: \(g(w)>0\)

Here \(J(w)=\infty\), while \(L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha g(w)\) is a finite number:

$$L(w,\alpha)<\infty=J(w)$$
$$L(w,\alpha)\;\le\;J(w)\qquad\text{for every }w\text{ and every fixed }\alpha\ge0$$

Step 4 — minimise both sides

Why are we allowed to do this?

Because taking minima preserves an inequality that holds everywhere. If the graph of \(L\) lies on or below the graph of \(J\) at every single point, then the lowest point \(L\) ever reaches cannot sit higher than the lowest point \(J\) ever reaches — any \(w\) that pulls \(J\) down pulls \(L\) at least as far down at the same place.

Written out: let \(w'\) be a minimiser of \(J\). Then \(\min_w L(w,\alpha)\le L(w',\alpha)\le J(w')=\min_w J(w)\). The first step holds because a minimum is no larger than any particular value, the second is step 3.

One caution: this works in one direction only. Minimising both sides is safe; maximising both sides of a pointwise inequality is not, because the two functions may peak at different places.

$$\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)\;\le\;\min_{w}J(w)=f\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

Step 5 — take the best lower bound

That inequality holds for every fixed \(\alpha\ge0\), and the right-hand side does not depend on \(\alpha\) at all. So each \(\alpha\) hands us a lower bound on the primal optimum, and we may keep the largest of them:

$$\max_{\alpha\ge 0}\,\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)\;\le\;f\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

Step 6 — name the inner minimisation

The inner part is exactly the dual function, \(q(\alpha)=\min_w L(w,\alpha)\). Substituting it, and writing \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) for the maximiser:

$$q\bigl(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\bigr)\;=\;\max_{\alpha\ge0}q(\alpha)\;=\;d^\star\;\le\;p^\star\;=\;f\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)$$

The best the dual can do never beats the best the primal can do. That is weak duality.

StepStatementReason
1\(\min_w J(w)=f(w^{\text{opt}})\)an infinite penalty rules out infeasible \(w\)
2\(L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha g(w)\)a finite penalty instead — a relaxation
3\(L(w,\alpha)\le J(w)\)\(\alpha g(w)\le0\) when feasible; finite \(<\infty\) when not
4\(\min_w L(w,\alpha)\le f(w^{\text{opt}})\)minima preserve a pointwise inequality
5\(\max_{\alpha\ge0}\min_w L\le f(w^{\text{opt}})\)true for each \(\alpha\), so true for the best one
6\(q(\alpha^{\text{opt}})\le f(w^{\text{opt}})\)\(q(\alpha)\) is the name of \(\min_w L(w,\alpha)\)
What the proof never used

No step asked \(f\) or \(g\) to be convex, smooth, or even continuous. Step 3 needed only the sign of \(\alpha g(w)\), and step 4 needed only that minima preserve order. This is why weak duality is unconditional, and why closing the gap — strong duality — requires genuinely extra assumptions.

Where exactly would the proof break if \(\alpha\) were allowed to be negative?

At step 3, case 1. With \(\alpha<0\) and \(g(w)\le0\), the product \(\alpha g(w)\) is non-negative, so \(L(w,\alpha)\ge f(w)=J(w)\) and the inequality flips on the feasible region. Everything downstream reverses with it, and \(q(\alpha)\) stops being a lower bound. The sign restriction \(\alpha\ge0\) is not bookkeeping — it is the single assumption the whole result stands on.

Strong duality: when the gap closes

When \(d^\star=p^\star\) we have strong duality, and solving the dual is as good as solving the primal. The standard sufficient condition is:

  • \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are convex, and
  • Slater's condition holds: some \(w\) satisfies every constraint strictly, \(g_i(w)<0\). When the constraints are affine, as they are for the SVM, plain feasibility is enough.
PrimalDual
Form\(\min_w\max_{\alpha\ge0}L\)\(\max_{\alpha\ge0}\min_w L\)
Optimised variable\(w\) (outer)\(\alpha\) (outer)
Optimal value\(p^\star\)\(d^\star\le p^\star\) always
Shapeconvex if \(f,g\) areconcave in \(\alpha\), always
Equal when\(f,g\) convex and Slater's condition holds

This is why the lecture checked all this before touching the SVM: the SVM primal will turn out to be convex with affine constraints, so we are free to solve its dual instead — and the dual is easier.

Why the dual function is concave

We claimed earlier that \(q(\alpha)=\min_w L(w,\alpha)\) is always concave, whatever \(f\) and \(g\) are. The reason is structural. For a fixed \(w\), the Lagrangian is an affine function of \(\alpha\):

$$L(w,\alpha)=\underbrace{f(w)}_{\text{intercept}}+\alpha\,\underbrace{g(w)}_{\text{slope}}$$

Each \(w\) therefore contributes one straight line in the \(\alpha\) plane, and \(q\) takes the lowest of them at every \(\alpha\). Two rules of convex analysis govern what survives that operation:

OperationRuleResult for lines
pointwise maximumthe max of convex functions is convexupper envelope is convex
pointwise minimumthe min of concave functions is concavelower envelope is concave

An affine function qualifies under both rules, since it is simultaneously convex and concave. But \(q\) is built with a minimum, so only the second rule applies to it: it inherits concavity and keeps no claim on convexity.

The same lines, two envelopes

Both panels below draw the identical family of lines. The left traces their upper boundary, the right their lower boundary. Drag the chord endpoints and the weight \(\lambda\), and read the verdict under each.

Upper envelope — \(\max_i\,(a_i t+b_i)\)

Lower envelope — \(\min_i\,(a_i t+b_i)\)

Where the dual's lines come from

  • How the Lines are Created: Let's use a specific example where the main cost formula is \(f(w) = w^2\) and the rule is \(g(w) = 1 - w\). Every number you pick for \(w\) draws exactly one straight line on the graph. The formula \(f(w)\) dictates where the line starts on the vertical axis (its intercept), and \(g(w)\) dictates the angle of the line (its slope).
  • The Big Picture: Think of every single straight line as a different choice of \(w\) stating: "If you make the penalty price \(\alpha\), my total score will be \(L(w, \alpha)\)". The dual function is just the system shopping for the best (lowest) offer at every single price point. By tracing the bottom edge of all these infinitely many straight lines, it automatically forms a smooth, downward-bending curve. The curve happens naturally, even though not a single line used to build it actually curves.
Why this matters for block 5

Concavity of \(q\) holds no matter how badly behaved \(f\) and \(g\) are, because it depends only on \(L\) being affine in \(\alpha\) — which it is by construction. So the dual problem \(\max_{\alpha\ge0}q(\alpha)\) never has a local maximum that is not global, and a solver that climbs \(q\) can be trusted to find \(d^\star\). The primal may be a nightmare; the dual is always a well-posed concave maximisation. Case 4 of the visualiser above shows exactly that: a doubly non-convex problem whose \(q\) curve is still a clean dome.

If every \(L(\cdot,\alpha)\) is affine, why is \(q\) not affine too — or at least convex?

Because \(q\) is not one of those functions; it is the lower boundary of all of them at once. At any given \(\alpha\) a different \(w\) may be the winner, and the switch from one winner to the next is where the kink appears. Each kink of a lower envelope bends downwards, since the incoming line has the larger slope and the outgoing one the smaller — slopes decrease from left to right along a lower envelope, which is precisely concavity. An upper envelope has increasing slopes and so bends upwards instead.

Which variable do we hold fixed?

There is only one Lagrangian,

$$L(w,\alpha)=f(w)+\alpha\,g(w),$$

and it is a surface over two variables. The primal and the dual are not two different functions: they are the same surface read in the two possible directions. Every confusing moment in this part of the theory comes from losing track of which direction is in use, so here are all four slices in one place.

The two slices

Freeze one variable, let the other run, and you get a curve. Which kind of curve depends on which variable you froze.

Fix \(w\), vary \(\alpha\) → a straight line

With \(w\) locked, \(f(w)\) and \(g(w)\) are just two numbers, so

$$L(w,\alpha)=\underbrace{f(w)}_{\text{intercept}}+\alpha\,\underbrace{g(w)}_{\text{slope}}$$

is affine in \(\alpha\). Always a line, no exceptions.

Fix \(\alpha\), vary \(w\) → a curve

With \(\alpha\) locked, you are looking at the function

$$w\;\longmapsto\;f(w)+\alpha\,g(w)$$

which bends however \(f\) and \(g\) bend. It is a line only in the special case where both of them are affine in \(w\).

The four cases

Each slice does one job for the primal and a different job for the dual. Two of the four are what the algorithm actually computes; the other two are how we picture what it is computing.

CaseSliceRoleWhat it gives you
1. Dualfix \(\alpha\), vary \(w\)operationalcomputes \(q(\alpha)=\min_w L(w,\alpha)\) — one number per price
2. Dualfix \(w\), vary \(\alpha\)structuralthe family of straight lines whose lower envelope is \(q\)
3. Primalfix \(\alpha\), vary \(w\)structuralthe family of curves whose upper envelope is \(J\)
4. Primalfix \(w\), vary \(\alpha\)operationalcomputes \(J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)\) — one number per choice of \(w\)

Notice the pattern. Cases 1 and 4 are the inner operations of the dual and the primal: whichever variable belongs to the inner optimisation is the one that varies, while the outer one waits. Cases 2 and 3 take the opposite slice and sweep it, collecting a whole family instead of a single number — which is how each envelope gets built.

Case 1 — fix \(\alpha\), vary \(w\): computing the dual

This is the step a solver performs. Lock the price first — say \(\alpha=0.8\) — then search over \(w\) for the lowest total score. That score is \(q(0.8)\). Do it again at another price and you get another point; sweep every \(\alpha\ge0\) and you have traced the whole dual function.

One detail matters more than it looks: the search over \(w\) is unconstrained. Infeasible choices compete alongside feasible ones, because the constraint has been replaced by a finite charge rather than a prohibition. That is exactly why \(q(\alpha)\) can land below \(p^\star\) — an infeasible \(w\) may win the relaxed contest — and therefore why a duality gap is possible at all.

Case 2 — fix \(w\), vary \(\alpha\): the lines behind \(q\)

Freeze a single choice \(w\) and ask what its score does as the price rises. The answer is the straight line above: it starts at \(f(w)\) and climbs or falls at rate \(g(w)\). Each \(w\) contributes one such line — an offer that says "at price \(\alpha\), I deliver \(L(w,\alpha)\)."

Let \(w\) range over everything and you have an infinite family of lines. At every price the dual keeps the cheapest offer, so \(q\) is the lower envelope of that family. Lower envelopes of lines bend downwards, which is why \(q\) is concave no matter how badly behaved \(f\) and \(g\) are.

Case 3 — fix \(\alpha\), vary \(w\): the curves behind \(J\)

Take the same slice as case 1, but now sweep it across many prices instead of stopping at one. Each \(\alpha\) draws one curve over \(w\): the relaxed objective at that price. The barrier is what you get by taking the highest curve at every \(w\):

$$J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)=\begin{cases}f(w), & g(w)\le 0\\ \infty, & g(w)>0\end{cases}$$

So \(J\) is the upper envelope of the family of curves, exactly mirroring \(q\) as the lower envelope of the family of lines. And since an upper envelope of convex functions is convex, this also explains why the primal stays convex whenever \(f\) and every \(g_i\) are — the maximum rule of block 5d, applied along the other axis.

Case 4 — fix \(w\), vary \(\alpha\): computing the barrier

The primal's inner step maximises a single line over \(\alpha\ge0\), and a line needs no search — its slope settles it. If \(g(w)\le0\) the line falls or stays flat, so the best price is \(\alpha=0\) and the value is \(f(w)\). If \(g(w)>0\) the line climbs without bound and the value is \(\infty\). That is the two-case barrier, read straight off the slope.

Putting it together

PrimalDual
Inner stepfix \(w\), maximise over \(\alpha\)fix \(\alpha\), minimise over \(w\)
Family it sweepscurves in \(w\), one per \(\alpha\)lines in \(\alpha\), one per \(w\)
Envelope takenupperlower
Result\(J(w)\), convex if \(f,g\) are\(q(\alpha)\), concave always
Cost of the inner stepfree — read the slopea real optimisation over \(w\)
$$\underbrace{\min_{w}\;\overbrace{\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)}^{\text{case 4}\;\to\;J(w)}}_{\text{primal}}\qquad\qquad\underbrace{\max_{\alpha\ge0}\;\overbrace{\min_{w}L(w,\alpha)}^{\text{case 1}\;\to\;q(\alpha)}}_{\text{dual}}$$

Read either expression from the inside out and the slice is never ambiguous: the inner variable moves, the outer one waits its turn.

Why the dual is still worth forming

The last row of the table is an uneven trade. The primal's inner step is free, while the dual's is a genuine minimisation that must be solved afresh at every price. We accept that cost because of what it buys: the outer problem becomes a concave maximisation with nothing but \(\alpha\ge0\) to respect — no local maxima, no awkward constraints. For the SVM in Part C it also drops the dimension from \(d\) to \(n\) and exposes the data only through inner products.

In panel A of the visualiser, why does dragging the \(\alpha\) slider move only the dashed curve and never the solid one?

The dashed curve is a case 1 slice — the relaxed objective \(L(\cdot,\alpha)\) at the slider's current price — so it tilts as the price changes. The solid curve is \(J(w)\), from which \(\alpha\) has already been eliminated by the inner maximisation of case 4; \(J\) is a function of \(w\) alone, so no setting of the slider can touch it. Weak duality is the statement that the dashed curve never rises above the solid one, wherever the slider sits. Sweeping the slider through every price and keeping the highest dashed curve at each \(w\) is case 3, and would rebuild the solid one.

horizontal: w  ·  vertical: value of L

the surface L(w, α)

horizontal: α  ·  vertical: value of L

5b

Seeing weak duality hold — and strong duality fail

Weak duality survives any \(f\) and any \(g\). Convexity is what upgrades it to equality.

The proof of block 5 never used a single property of \(f\) or \(g\). It is worth checking that claim against functions chosen to be as badly behaved as possible. Everything below works on a bounded domain \(w\in\mathcal W=[-2.5,\,2.5]\), which keeps both sides finite without changing any of the reasoning.

The three pictures

Start from the barrier function of block 3, written here as \(J\):

$$J(w)=\max_{\alpha\ge0}L(w,\alpha)=\begin{cases}f(w), & g(w)\le 0\\ \infty, & g(w)>0\end{cases}\qquad p^\star=\min_{w}J(w)$$

Fix any \(\alpha\ge0\). Then \(L(w,\alpha)\le J(w)\) at every \(w\): below the barrier because \(\alpha g(w)\le0\) there, and trivially below \(\infty\) outside it. Minimising both sides keeps the order, which gives \(q(\alpha)\le p^\star\), and taking the best \(\alpha\) gives \(d^\star\le p^\star\). The panels below show each step: the first is the pointwise comparison, the second is the sweep over \(\alpha\), and the third is the geometry that decides whether the gap closes.

objective convex
constraint convex

J(w) — the barrier, = f where feasible L(w, α) — the relaxed objective f(w) where it is infeasible J at your w L at your w q(α) = lowest point of L p* at wopt

Panel A — the pointwise comparison. Grey bands are where \(g(w)>0\), so \(J=\infty\) there.

q(α) = 0≤ L(w, α) = 0≤ J(w) = 0
p* = 0 d* = 0 gap = 0

Panel B — \(q(\alpha)\) never crosses \(p^\star\). The shaded band is the gap.

Panel C — achievable pairs \(\bigl(g(w),f(w)\bigr)\). Shaded half is feasible.

What to look for

  • Panel A, any case, any sliders. The dashed Lagrangian never climbs above the solid barrier, and the teal line \(q(\alpha)\) never climbs above the blue line \(p^\star\). That is weak duality, and no choice of case or slider breaks it.
  • Panel B, case 1. The \(q\) curve rises to touch \(p^\star\) exactly. Drag the shape slider anywhere: the gap readout stays at \(0.00\). Convexity plus a strictly feasible point makes this a theorem, not a coincidence.
  • Panel B, cases 2 to 4. The curve usually stops short of the line and the shaded band opens. Drag the shape slider and watch the gap grow and shrink — in some positions it closes completely. Non-convexity does not cause a gap; it merely withdraws the guarantee against one.
  • Panel C is the reason. Each \(w\) contributes one point \(\bigl(g(w),f(w)\bigr)\). The primal looks only at the shaded feasible half and takes the lowest point there, \(p^\star\). The dual slides a line of slope \(-\alpha\) underneath the whole set and reads its height at the vertical axis, \(q(\alpha)\). When the set bulges inward, no straight line can reach into the dent, and the best line stops below \(p^\star\) — that shortfall is the gap. In case 1 the set has no dent on its lower-left boundary, so a line reaches \(p^\star\) exactly.
The honest statement

Convexity with Slater's condition is sufficient for \(d^\star=p^\star\), never necessary. Cases 2 to 4 can and sometimes do close their gap — the shape slider shows it happening. What they lose is the certificate: without convexity you must check the number, while in case 1 you may simply solve the dual and trust it. That is precisely the licence Part C uses for the SVM.

In case 1, set the shape slider so the constraint is inactive. What happens to \(\alpha^\star\), and why does panel C make it obvious?

\(\alpha^\star\) drops to zero. The unconstrained minimiser already lies in the feasible half, so the lowest point of the whole achievable set is also the lowest feasible point. A horizontal line — slope \(-\alpha=0\) — supports the set there and already reaches \(p^\star\); tilting it would only lower where it meets the axis. This is complementary slackness seen sideways: a constraint that does not bind carries no price.

6

Complementary slackness and the KKT conditions

At the optimum, every constraint is either tight or free — never both slack and priced.

Assume strong duality, and let \(w^{\text{opt}}\) solve the primal and \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\) solve the dual. Substitute each into its own problem:

$$\max_{\alpha\ge0}\bigl(f(w^{\text{opt}})+\alpha\,g(w^{\text{opt}})\bigr)\;=\;\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\bigr)$$

On the left, \(w^{\text{opt}}\) is feasible, so by block 3 the maximum is simply \(f(w^{\text{opt}})\):

$$f(w^{\text{opt}})=\min_{w}\bigl(f(w)+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w)\bigr)$$

The right side is the minimum of \(L(w,\alpha^{\text{opt}})\) over all \(w\). The particular point \(w^{\text{opt}}\) is one of the candidates, but not necessarily the minimiser, so its value is at least as large as the minimum:

$$f(w^{\text{opt}})\;\le\;f(w^{\text{opt}})+\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\ge 0\quad (1)$$

But the constraints themselves say \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\ge 0\) and \(g(w^{\text{opt}})\le 0\), so their product satisfies

$$\alpha^{\text{opt}}g(w^{\text{opt}})\le 0\quad (2)$$

Inequalities (1) and (2) can hold together only if the product is zero:

$$\alpha^{\text{opt}}\cdot g\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)=0\qquad\text{(complementary slackness)}$$

Read it as a pair of alternatives:

  • Either the multiplier is zero: the constraint is inactive and could be deleted without changing the answer
  • Or \(g(w^{\text{opt}})=0\), the constraint is active and the solution sits exactly on its boundary.
Both factors may be zero at once.

With several constraints the same argument gives \(\sum_i\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}g_i(w^{\text{opt}})\ge0\) while every term is \(\le 0\), so each term vanishes separately: \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}g_i(w^{\text{opt}})=0\) for every \(i\).

Slater's condition

Slater's condition is a foundational rule in convex optimization that, when satisfied, guarantees strong duality: meaning the duality gap between the primal problem and the dual problem is exactly zero (\(p^\star = d^\star\)).

For a problem to satisfy Slater's condition, it must meet two requirements:

  1. Convexity: The problem itself must be inherently convex. This means the objective function \(f(w)\) and all inequality constraints \(g_i(w)\) must be convex functions (structurally shaped without any concave "dents").
  2. Strict Feasibility: There must exist at least one point in the domain that strictly satisfies all non-linear inequality constraints. Rather than just barely following the rules by riding the absolute boundary (where \(g_i(w) = 0\)), this point must fall safely inside the legal zone (where \(g_i(w) < 0\)).

In simple terms, if a problem is convex and possesses some mathematical "wiggle room" inside its constraints, Slater's condition ensures that the primal and dual optimal values will perfectly align.

The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions

While complementary slackness provides a crucial link between constraints and their penalty prices, it is only one piece of a larger mathematical puzzle. To definitively prove that a specific coordinate pair \((w^\star, \alpha^\star)\) is the optimal solution, it must pass a complete, four-part diagnostic test known as the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions. For convex problems that successfully satisfy Slater's condition, this four-step checklist provides an absolute mathematical guarantee. Under these conditions, the KKT rules become both necessary (if a point is the true optimum, it is mathematically forced to pass all four tests) and sufficient (if any point passes all four tests, it is guaranteed to be the true global optimum).

ConditionStatementWhere it comes from
Stationarity\(\nabla f(w^\star)+\sum_i\alpha_i^\star\nabla g_i(w^\star)=0\)\(w^\star\) minimises \(L(w,\alpha^\star)\)
Primal feasibility\(g_i(w^\star)\le 0\) for all \(i\)the original constraints
Dual feasibility\(\alpha_i^\star\ge 0\) for all \(i\)the multipliers' sign
Complementary slackness\(\alpha_i^\star\,g_i(w^\star)=0\) for all \(i\)the argument above

For the SVM, stationarity will give the formula for \(w\) (block 14) and complementary slackness will identify the support vectors (block 17).

Part B
The maximum-margin problem
7

Many separators, one margin

A linearly separable dataset has infinitely many separating lines. Which one should we prefer?

\(\lVert w\rVert\)
\(\gamma\) — functional, the band's label
\(\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\) — geometric half-width
\(2\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\) — band width
closest point's \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\) — functional
closest point's distance — geometric

Here is one dataset with three separating lines, each drawn with its margin band \(w^{\top}x=\pm\gamma\):

All three classify the training data perfectly. Intuitively, separator 3 is the best: its band is widest, so a new point that lands a little away from its class's training points is still likely to fall on the correct side. The perceptron gives a formal version of that intuition.

The perceptron's mistake bound

If the data is separable with margin \(\gamma\) and every point satisfies \(\lVert x_i\rVert\le R\), the number of mistakes \(l\) the perceptron makes before converging is bounded by

$$l\;\le\;\left(\frac{R}{\gamma}\right)^{2}$$

A larger margin means fewer mistakes. But the perceptron only guarantees that it will find some \(w\) that separates the data with some positive margin — which one depends on the initialisation and on the order the examples arrive in. It does not guarantee the \(w\) with the maximum margin. So we need a method that searches for that one explicitly.

Functional margin and geometric margin

Two different quantities are both called "margin". The functional margin of a point is \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\); the geometric margin is \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i/\lVert w\rVert\), the actual distance from the point to the line. In the mistake bound, \(\gamma\) is geometric (it assumes \(\lVert w\rVert=1\)). In the three figures, \(\gamma\) is functional: the dashed lines are \(w^{\top}x=\pm\gamma\), and the band's real half-width is \(\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\).

Separator\(w\)\(\gamma\) (functional)\(\lVert w\rVert\)half-width \(\gamma/\lVert w\rVert\)band width
1\([1,\,1]\)11.4140.7071.414
2\([1,\,0.5]\)1.51.1181.3422.683
3\([0.5,\,1]\)21.1181.7893.578

Here the ranking by \(\gamma\) happens to agree with the ranking by true width. In general it need not: \(\gamma\) alone says nothing until \(\lVert w\rVert\) is pinned down. That observation is the whole of the next block.

8

The naive formulation is ill-posed

Maximise the margin, subject to every point clearing it. Written literally, this has no solution.

The direct translation of "find the boundary that maximises \(\gamma\)" is

$$\max_{w,\,\gamma}\;\gamma\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge\gamma\quad\forall i$$

Suppose \((w,\gamma)\) satisfies every constraint. Multiply through by any \(c>0\):

$$y_i\,(cw)^{\top}x_i=c\,y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\;\ge\;c\gamma\qquad\forall i$$

so \((cw,\,c\gamma)\) satisfies them too. For \(c>1\) the objective has grown, \(c\gamma>\gamma\), yet the decision boundary \(\{x : (cw)^{\top}x=0\}\) is the same set of points as \(\{x : w^{\top}x=0\}\). Nothing about the geometry has changed.

Because the constraints allow a larger \(\gamma\) whenever \(w\) is scaled up, the optimisation drives both \(\gamma\) and \(\lVert w\rVert\) to infinity without ever changing the separator. The problem is unbounded — it has no optimal solution — and is called ill-posed. To make it meaningful we must remove the freedom to scale \(w\) arbitrarily. There are two ways to do it, in the next two blocks.

Where did the bias go?

The figure above includes a bias \(b\), but the lecture's algebra uses \(w^{\top}x\) alone, which describes a boundary through the origin. The usual justification is to append a constant feature, \(x\mapsto[x;\,1]\), so that the last weight plays the role of \(b\). That is fine for classification, but it means the norm \(\lVert w\rVert^2\) minimised later also includes \(b^2\), which is a slightly different problem from the standard SVM. The standard version keeps \(b\) separate; blocks 15 and 19 note what changes when it does.

9

Fix 1: fix the norm of w

Only allow weight vectors of unit length. Correct, but awkward to optimise.

Add the constraint \(\lVert w\rVert_2^2=1\). If \((w,\gamma)\) is feasible, the scaled pair \((cw,c\gamma)\) now has \(\lVert cw\rVert_2^2=c^2\lVert w\rVert_2^2=c^2\), which violates the constraint for every \(c\neq1\). Scaling is ruled out.

$$\max_{w,\,\gamma}\;\gamma\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge\gamma\ \ \forall i\qquad\text{and}\qquad\lVert w\rVert_2^2=1$$

With a unit-length \(w\), \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\) is the true distance of \(x_i\) from the boundary, so \(\gamma\) is now the geometric margin. The formulation is correct. It is just inconvenient:

  • We optimise over two kinds of variable, \(w\) and \(\gamma\), coupled through every constraint.
  • The set \(\{w : \lVert w\rVert=1\}\) is a sphere, which is not a convex set: the midpoint of two unit vectors is shorter than 1. An equality constraint keeps a problem convex only if it is affine. Without convexity, the duality results of block 5 are no longer guaranteed, and it is the dual we want to solve later.
An aside

Relaxing the equality to \(\lVert w\rVert\le 1\) makes the problem convex again, because the unit ball is a convex set, and the optimum always lands on its boundary anyway. The lecture takes a different route, which leads to a cleaner objective.

10

Fix 2: fix the functional margin to 1

Instead of fixing the length of \(w\), fix the value of \(\gamma\) — and let the length of \(w\) carry the information.

A three-dimensional example

Take \(w=[2,\,4,\,3]\) and \(\gamma=10\), so \(w^{\top}x=2x_1+4x_2+3x_3\). The three planes \(w^{\top}x=10\), \(w^{\top}x=0\) and \(w^{\top}x=-10\) are parallel, each perpendicular to \(w\).

The distance between two parallel planes \(w^{\top}x=0\) and \(w^{\top}x=\gamma\) follows from moving along the unit normal. Start at any \(x_0\) with \(w^{\top}x_0=0\) and step a distance \(t\) in the direction \(w/\lVert w\rVert\):

$$w^{\top}\Bigl(x_0+t\,\frac{w}{\lVert w\rVert}\Bigr)=0+t\,\frac{w^{\top}w}{\lVert w\rVert}=t\,\lVert w\rVert=\gamma\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad t=\frac{\gamma}{\lVert w\rVert}$$

Here \(\operatorname{len}(\overline{AB})=\operatorname{len}(\overline{CD})=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{2^2+4^2+3^2}}=\dfrac{10}{\sqrt{29}}\approx1.857\).

Rescaling so that \(\gamma=1\)

Now divide \(w\) by \(10\). With \(w_{\text{new}}=w/10\), the same three planes are described by

$$\frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{10}{10}=1,\qquad \frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{0}{10}=0,\qquad \frac{w^{\top}}{10}x=\frac{-10}{10}=-1.$$

This is always possible. Whichever \(w\) separates the dataset, it can be rescaled so that the closest points satisfy \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i=1\) exactly — a canonical scaling. So we may require

$$y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\qquad\forall i$$

Different separators need different rescalings

Applying the same idea to separators 2 and 3 from block 8:

Separatordivide \(w\) by\(w_{\text{new}}\)\(\lVert w_{\text{new}}\rVert\)half-width \(1/\lVert w_{\text{new}}\rVert\)
11\([1,\,1]\)1.4140.707
21.5\([0.667,\,0.333]\)0.7451.342
32\([0.25,\,0.5]\)0.5591.789
The key observation

A larger margin means dividing \(w\) by a larger number, which makes \(w_{\text{new}}\) smaller. Once the functional margin is fixed at 1, the width of the band is controlled entirely by \(\lVert w\rVert\): the smaller the weight vector, the wider the margin.

11

Maximum width and the convex primal

Among all canonically scaled separators, choose the one with the widest band.

Every separating \(w\) can be scaled to satisfy \(y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\). We prefer the one that leaves the most room between the two margin lines:

$$\max_{w}\;\operatorname{margin-width}\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\quad\forall i$$

From block 11, each margin line is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\) from the boundary, so the width between \(w^{\top}x=1\) and \(w^{\top}x=-1\) is \(2/\lVert w\rVert\).

So we maximise \(2/\lVert w\rVert\). Equivalently we may maximise \(2/\lVert w\rVert^2\): squaring is strictly increasing for positive numbers, so both objectives are largest at the same \(w\). And maximising a positive quantity is the same as minimising its reciprocal:

$$\max_{w}\frac{2}{\lVert w\rVert^2}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\min_{w}\frac{\lVert w\rVert^2}{2}$$
$$\min_{w}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,\bigl(w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\ge 1\quad\forall i$$

This is the hard-margin SVM primal. The objective is a convex quadratic; each constraint is affine in \(w\). It is a quadratic program with a unique optimal \(w\), and it has a feasible point exactly when the data is linearly separable. The factor \(\tfrac12\) changes nothing about the answer; it is there so that the gradient of the objective is simply \(w\).

With a separate bias the primal reads \(\min_{w,b}\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) subject to \(y_i\,(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge1\). Only \(w\) is penalised, so shifting the boundary is free and only tilting it costs.

Why minimise \(\lVert w\rVert^2\) instead of \(\lVert w\rVert\), when both give the same \(w\)?

\(\lVert w\rVert\) has a kink at \(w=0\) and a gradient \(w/\lVert w\rVert\) that is awkward to work with. \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) is smooth everywhere with gradient \(w\), which is what makes the inner minimisation in block 14 a one-line calculation and turns the whole problem into a standard quadratic program.

Part C
The dual and the support vectors
12

The SVM in Lagrangian form

Rewrite the primal in the standard shape of block 1, and Part A applies directly.

The SVM primal is solvable as it stands — it is a quadratic program. But looking at it through the Lagrangian lens gives a problem that is often easier and, more importantly, far more revealing. First, match it to the standard form \(\min_w f(w)\) s.t. \(g_i(w)\le0\):

StepForm
Primal from block 12\(\min_w \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1\ \ \forall i\)
Constraints moved to "\(\le 0\)"\(\min_w \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ 1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\le 0\ \ \forall i\)
Matched to the standard form\(f(w)=\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2,\qquad g_i(w)=1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\)

There is one constraint per training point, so there are \(n\) multipliers \(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\). The primal in min–max form is

$$\min_{w}\;\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\Bigl(\,{\color{#4A1E5C}\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2}\;+\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\color{#1F8A85}\alpha_i}\,{\color{#B23A6B}\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)}\Bigr)$$
objective \(f(w)\)Small \(\lVert w\rVert\) means a wide margin.
multiplier \(\alpha_i\)One price per training point, \(\alpha_i\ge0\).
constraint \(g_i(w)\)Positive exactly when point \(i\) is inside the margin or misclassified.

Is swapping to the dual allowed? \(f\) is convex, every \(g_i\) is affine, and for separable data a feasible \(w\) exists. By block 5, strong duality holds, so the dual has the same optimal value:

$$\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\min_{w}\;\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\Bigr)$$
13

Solving the inner minimisation

For fixed multipliers, the best \(w\) is a weighted sum of the training points.

Fix \(\vec\alpha\) — say \(n=3\) and \(\alpha_1=3,\ \alpha_2=0,\ \alpha_3=8\). What remains is

$$\min_{w}\;\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,\bigl(1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\bigr)\Bigr)$$

This is an unconstrained minimisation over \(w\) of a convex, differentiable function — the same situation as finding the \(w\) that minimises squared loss in linear regression. So we differentiate with respect to \(w\) and set the result to zero. Expanding the sum first:

$$\frac{\partial}{\partial w}\Bigl(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\Bigr)=w-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,x_i=0$$
$$\vec w_{\alpha}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i\,\vec x_i$$

This is the stationarity condition of block 7. With \(\alpha=(3,0,8)\) it gives \(w_\alpha=3y_1x_1+8y_3x_3\): the point \(x_2\) plays no part at all. That observation becomes the central result of block 17.

The result depends on \(\alpha\), and the outer problem is still to find the \(\alpha\) that maximises the objective. So the next step is to substitute \(w_\alpha\) back into the objective, leaving a function of \(\alpha\) alone.

Matrix form

Stack the data points as the rows of \(X\in\mathbb R^{n\times d}\), put the labels on the diagonal of \(Y=\operatorname{diag}(y_1,\dots,y_n)\), and collect the multipliers in \(\vec\alpha\in\mathbb R^{n}\). Then \(X^{\top}\) has the data points as its columns, and

$$\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} w_{1}\\ w_{2}\\ \vdots\\ w_{d}\end{bmatrix}}_{d\times 1} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} x_{1,1} & x_{2,1} & \cdots & x_{n,1}\\ x_{1,2} & x_{2,2} & \cdots & x_{n,2}\\ \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots\\ x_{1,d} & x_{2,d} & \cdots & x_{n,d}\end{bmatrix}}_{d\times n\;=\;X^{\top}} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} y_1 & 0 & \cdots & 0\\ 0 & y_2 & \cdots & 0\\ \vdots & & \ddots & \vdots\\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & y_n\end{bmatrix}}_{n\times n\;=\;Y} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\alpha_1\\ \alpha_2\\ \vdots\\ \alpha_n\end{bmatrix}}_{n\times 1}$$

\(x_{i,j}\) is feature \(j\) of data point \(i\). Column \(i\) of \(X^{\top}\) is \(\vec x_i\); multiplying by \(Y\) scales it to \(y_i\vec x_i\), and multiplying by \(\vec\alpha\) sums the columns with weights \(\alpha_i\).

$$\vec w_{\alpha}=X^{\top}Y\,\vec\alpha$$
14

Back-substitution: the dual objective

Replace \(w\) by \(X^{\top}Y\vec\alpha\) everywhere, and the problem becomes a quadratic in \(\alpha\) alone.

In matrix notation, the vector with entries \(1-y_i\,x_i^{\top}w\) is \(\mathbf 1-YXw\), so the Lagrangian is

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)=\tfrac12\,w_\alpha^{\top}w_\alpha+\alpha^{\top}\bigl(\mathbf 1-YXw_\alpha\bigr)$$

Substituting \(w_\alpha=X^{\top}Y\alpha\):

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)={\color{#1F8A85}\tfrac12\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)}+{\color{#B8582A}\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1}-{\color{#B23A6B}\alpha^{\top}YX\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)}$$

Simplify each coloured term. Since \(Y\) is diagonal, \(Y^{\top}=Y\):

TermSimplification
①\(\tfrac12\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)^{\top}\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)=\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}Y^{\top}X\,X^{\top}Y\alpha=\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\)
②\(\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1=\sum_i\alpha_i\) — already as simple as it gets
③\(\alpha^{\top}YX\bigl(X^{\top}Y\alpha\bigr)=\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\) — the same quadratic form as ①, without the \(\tfrac12\)

So ① − ③ is \(\bigl(\tfrac12-1\bigr)\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha\), and

$$L(w_\alpha,\alpha)=\alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\,\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha$$

Maximising this over \(\alpha\ge0\) is the SVM dual. Written out with sums, which is how it usually appears in exam questions:

$$\max_{\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_n\ge 0}\;\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_i\alpha_j\,y_iy_j\,x_i^{\top}x_j$$

The matrix \(K=XX^{\top}\), with entries \(K_{ij}=x_i^{\top}x_j\), is the Gram matrix of the data. The matrix \(Q=YXX^{\top}Y=(YX)(YX)^{\top}\) is positive semi-definite, so \(-\tfrac12\alpha^{\top}Q\alpha\) is concave: the dual is a concave quadratic maximisation over the simple region \(\alpha\ge0\).

With a separate bias \(b\)

If the constraints are \(y_i(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge 1\), the Lagrangian gains a term \(-b\sum_i\alpha_i y_i\). Setting its derivative with respect to \(b\) to zero gives one extra condition, and the dual becomes the same objective with the constraints

$$\alpha_i\ge 0\ \ \forall i\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i\,y_i=0.$$

The second constraint says the total price on each class must balance. This is the form found in most textbooks and in library implementations.

15

Why the dual helps

The same problem, stated in terms of data points instead of features.

$$\min_{w}\ \tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\ \ \text{s.t.}\ \ y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\ge 1$$

Standard primal: \(d\) variables

$$\max_{\vec\alpha\ge 0}\ \alpha^{\top}\mathbf 1-\tfrac12\alpha^{\top}YXX^{\top}Y\alpha$$

Standard dual: \(n\) variables

The primal searches over \(w\in\mathbb R^{d}\), one variable per feature. The dual searches over \(\alpha\in\mathbb R^{n}\), one variable per training point. When \(d\gg n\) — text with a vocabulary of a million words and a few thousand documents, for instance — the dual solves the same problem in far fewer dimensions.

What the dual gains
  • Dimension \(n\) instead of \(d\).
  • Constraints are just \(\alpha_i\ge0\), instead of \(n\) coupled inequalities.
  • The data enters only through inner products \(x_i^{\top}x_j\), which is what makes kernels possible (block 21).
  • Most \(\alpha_i\) come out exactly zero (block 17), so the solution is sparse.
What it costs
  • The Gram matrix is \(n\times n\): memory grows as \(n^2\).
  • When \(n\gg d\), the primal is the smaller problem.
  • \(w\) is not produced directly; it has to be rebuilt from \(\alpha\) through \(w=X^{\top}Y\alpha\).
16

Complementary slackness: the support vectors

Only the points on the margin get a non-zero price. They alone determine \(w\).

From block 14, the optimal weight vector is a linear combination of the data points, with the importance of point \(i\) given by \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\ge 0\):

$$\vec w_{\alpha^{\text{opt}}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\,y_i\,\vec x_i$$

Some \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\) may be zero and others positive. Which ones? Apply complementary slackness (block 7) to the SVM constraint \(g_i(w)=1-y_i\,w^{\top}x_i\):

$$\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\times\Bigl(1-y_i\,\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)^{\top}x_i\Bigr)=0\qquad\forall i$$

Each product is zero, which leaves two readings:

If \(\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}>0\)
$$1-y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i=0$$ $$\Rightarrow\ y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i=1$$

The point lies exactly on its margin line.

If \(y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i>1\)
$$1-y_i\,(w^{\text{opt}})^{\top}x_i<0$$ $$\Rightarrow\ \alpha_i^{\text{opt}}=0$$

The point is strictly beyond its margin line and contributes nothing.

Only points on the margin can have \(\alpha_i>0\), so only they contribute to \(w^{\text{opt}}\). These points are called support vectors — they "support" the margin the way the posts support a fence — and the algorithm is the support vector machine. The rest of the training set could be thrown away after training.

Note:

The implication runs one way. The conclusion is: "only the points on the gamma margin will have alpha > 0". That doesn't mean that if a point lies on the margin, its corresponding alpha is always greater than 0. The logic gives \(\alpha_i>0\Rightarrow\) on the margin, but not the converse: a point can lie exactly on the margin and still have \(\alpha_i=0\), because both factors of the product may be zero. Support vectors are the points with \(\alpha_i>0\); they all lie on the margin, but not every margin point must be one. When several margin points are collinear, as in the figure, the optimal \(\alpha\) is often not unique even though \(w\) is (block 18 shows this).

17

Training and prediction

Everything above reduces to two phases.

Training phase

  1. Solve the dual QP of block 15 for \(\alpha^{\text{opt}}\).
  2. Compute \(w^{\text{opt}}=\sum_i\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}y_ix_i\). Only the support vectors (\(\alpha_i>0\)) enter the sum.

Testing phase

For a new point \(x_{\text{test}}\), compute

$$f(x_{\text{test}})=\bigl(w^{\text{opt}}\bigr)^{\top}x_{\text{test}}=\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{SV}}\alpha_i^{\text{opt}}\,y_i\;x_i^{\top}x_{\text{test}}$$
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})>0\), predict \(y=+1\).
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})<0\), predict \(y=-1\).
  • If \(f(x_{\text{test}})=0\) the point lies on the boundary itself and the label is a tie, broken by convention.

The second form of \(f\) needs only the support vectors and inner products with them. The magnitude \(|f(x_{\text{test}})|/\lVert w\rVert\) is the test point's distance from the boundary, a natural measure of how confident the prediction is.

Part D
Beyond the hard margin
18

Soft margin

The hard-margin SVM has no solution at all if a single point is on the wrong side. Real data needs slack.

Beyond the slides

Blocks 20 and 21 are not in the lecture. They are the two standard extensions that make SVMs usable in practice, and they reuse every idea above.

Give each point a slack variable \(\xi_i\ge0\) that measures how far it falls short of the margin, and charge for it:

$$\min_{w,\,b,\,\xi}\;\frac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_{i=1}^{n}\xi_i\qquad\text{s.t.}\qquad y_i\,(w^{\top}x_i+b)\ge 1-\xi_i,\quad \xi_i\ge 0$$
  • \(C\) trades width against violations. A large \(C\) makes violations expensive and approaches the hard margin; a small \(C\) accepts some violations in exchange for a wider, more robust band.
  • The dual barely changes. Repeating blocks 14–15 gives the same objective with the box constraint \(0\le\alpha_i\le C\) (plus \(\sum_i\alpha_iy_i=0\) with a bias).
  • Complementary slackness now has three cases. \(\alpha_i=0\): beyond the margin. \(0<\alpha_i<C\): exactly on the margin. \(\alpha_i=C\): inside the band or misclassified.
  • Hinge loss. At the optimum \(\xi_i=\max\bigl(0,\,1-y_if(x_i)\bigr)\), so the soft-margin SVM is regularised hinge-loss minimisation: \(\min_w\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2+C\sum_i\max(0,1-y_if(x_i))\).
19

Kernels

The dual only ever asks for inner products — so it never needs the features themselves.

In the dual objective and in the prediction rule, the data appears only as \(x_i^{\top}x_j\) and \(x_i^{\top}x_{\text{test}}\). If we first map each point through a feature map \(\phi\), all we need is \(\phi(x_i)^{\top}\phi(x_j)\). A kernel computes that number directly:

$$k(x,z)=\phi(x)^{\top}\phi(z),\qquad f(x_{\text{test}})=\sum_{i\,\in\,\text{SV}}\alpha_i\,y_i\,k(x_i,x_{\text{test}})+b$$
Kernel\(k(x,z)\)Implicit feature space
Linear\(x^{\top}z\)the original features — the SVM of these notes
Polynomial\((x^{\top}z+c)^p\)all monomials up to degree \(p\)
Gaussian (RBF)\(\exp\bigl(-\lVert x-z\rVert^2/2\sigma^2\bigr)\)infinite-dimensional

With the RBF kernel the primal would need an infinite-dimensional \(w\) and cannot even be written down, but the dual is still an \(n\)-variable quadratic program. This is the strongest argument for the dual formulation of block 16. A function is a valid kernel exactly when every Gram matrix it produces is positive semi-definite (Mercer's condition), which keeps the dual concave.

The whole chain in one line

Maximise the margin → fix the scale so the margin is \(1/\lVert w\rVert\) → minimise \(\tfrac12\lVert w\rVert^2\) under affine constraints → strong duality lets us solve the dual instead → stationarity writes \(w\) as a weighted sum of data points → complementary slackness zeroes every weight except those of the support vectors → the dual depends on the data only through inner products, which kernels generalise.
